claims.text: The target materials are solid, single-phase high-entropy alloys with varying compositional complexity and high configurational entropy.
An integrated protocol combining metadynamics and thermodynamic integration can determine solid-liquid transition properties in HEAs.
Metadynamics overcomes high-energy barriers and facilitates exploration of solid-liquid transition paths.
Thermodynamic integration provides accurate free-energy differences across the melting transition.
Mapping the free-energy landscape connecting solid and liquid phases permits extraction of latent thermodynamic parameters.
Enhanced sampling expedites rare-event barrier crossing.
Efficient integration over the sampled free-energy surface yields solid-liquid thermodynamic quantities.
Enthalpic and entropic contributions, including configurational entropy, influence phase stability in chemically disordered HEAs.
The protocol can accurately determine HEA melting temperatures.
The protocol can accurately determine HEA enthalpies and entropies of fusion.
The protocol can resolve volume changes at melting.
The protocol can determine key liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Errors in predicted melting temperature and fusion properties will be on the order of a few percent.
Predictions will agree closely with high-precision DSC and in-situ diffraction measurements.
The approach is applicable across a broad compositional range of HEAs.
The accuracy of the approach depends on interatomic potentials that reliably capture near-melting anharmonic effects.
The approach may fail when quantum, extreme anharmonic, electronic, or magnetic effects are not captured by the potential.
Standard calorimetry and narrow-range computational phase-diagram evaluations lack either broad applicability or sufficient resolution for complex HEA free-energy contributions.
Consistent discrepancies greater than 5% between simulations and experimental melting and fusion properties across multiple HEAs would falsify the approach.
